planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; provide a small moss pole if training upright, though most growers let it trail from a basket or shelf.

directions: 'Argyraeus' is the original, most widely distributed form of Scindapsus pictus sold in cultivation, and it carries the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its reliability. Compared to the heavily blotched 'Exotica' and 'Silvery Ann' selections, its narrower, more pointed, pine-green leaves show only modest, scattered silver flecking rather than large confluent silver patches, giving the plant a quieter, finer-textured look. Vines are slightly daintier and slower to bulk up than the heavily variegated cultivars, but the leathery, satin-surfaced foliage is just as tolerant of average indoor humidity. In its native Southeast Asian forests it presses juvenile leaves flat against tree bark in a shingling habit, though almost all cultivated specimens are grown as trailing or lightly climbing houseplants.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plants Award of Garden Merit list

planting.note: Provide a moss pole or trellis and strong, bright indirect light from day one; variegated sectors carry less chlorophyll, so growth is noticeably slower than plain-leaf Mini Monstera and low light causes reversion to solid green.

directions: This chimeral sport of the standard Mini Monstera breaks its deeply fenestrated leaves into irregular sectors of white or cream alongside the normal green, with the exact pattern varying from leaf to leaf and sometimes covering half a blade or more. Because the white tissue cannot photosynthesize, plants grow markedly slower than their all-green counterparts and demand more light to compensate, while overly bright direct sun can scorch the thin, chlorophyll-poor patches. Its scarcity and slow propagation rate (cuttings must retain a stable variegated node) have made it one of the most expensive houseplants on the market, with well-variegated specimens fetching prices far beyond ordinary aroids. Prune reverted, fully green shoots promptly to keep the plant's variegated growth dominant.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Rhaphidophora tetrasperma

planting.note: Attach young growth to cork bark, a bark panel, or a terrarium backwall in high humidity; this species roots in readily and will keep shingling as it climbs, even growing back down after it reaches the top of its support.

directions: Rhaphidophora pachyphylla is a small-growing Bornean shingling aroid distinguished from the papery, silvery Rhaphidophora cryptantha by its thicker, stiffer, more leathery deep-green leaves that stay closely overlapped against bark or a terrarium backwall. Unlike many Rhaphidophora that transform into large, differently shaped adult leaves once they mature, this species is neotenic and keeps its compact juvenile leaf form for life, making it a permanently small-scale shingler rather than an eventual large climbing vine. Its dense, tightly packed growth and tolerance of enclosed, humid conditions have made it a favorite backdrop plant for bioactive vivariums and terrariums, though it also does well mounted in a warm, shaded greenhouse setting. Keep the substrate around the roots evenly moist but never soggy, and maintain warmth and humidity year-round since it has little tolerance for dry air or cool drafts.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew) — Rhaphidophora pachyphylla
International Aroid Society — The Genus Rhaphidophora

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect to low light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Maggy is one of the more shade- and neglect-tolerant Homalomena selections, making it a common low-light office plant.

directions: 'Maggy' produces broad, rounded, very glossy heart-shaped leaves in a uniform deep green, without the reddish petioles that mark the similar 'Selby' selection or the fanned leaf ribbing of 'Emerald Gem,' giving it a plainer, glossier, almost lacquered look overall. Its dense, low, clumping rosette and unusually strong tolerance of low indoor light have made it a popular mass-market foliage plant sold under simply 'Homalomena' at big box retailers, valued as much for its air-purifying reputation as for its tidy houseplant form. It stays non-climbing and compact, needing no support, and is easily refreshed by division of the clump. Keep it out of cold drafts and below 55°F, and let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings.
sources: Costa Farms Plant Finder — Homalomena reference

planting.note: Provide a moss pole or trellis in bright indirect light to encourage the deep, early fenestrations this cultivar is grown for; trailing specimens without support stay smaller and unlobed.

directions: 'Baltic Blue' is a selected clone of Epipremnum pinnatum grown specifically for how readily its mature leaves fenestrate: given a climbing support and good light, it splits and perforates along the midrib earlier and more dramatically than the standard species or the similar 'Cebu Blue' form. Its foliage runs darker, richer green with a cooler blue-black cast rather than 'Cebu Blue's silvery, almost metallic sheen, and the leaf blades tend to be a bit narrower and more deeply cut once mature. Young, unsupported growth looks like an ordinary trailing pothos with small, solid, elongated leaves, so the plant's signature look only appears once it is trained to climb. Fast-growing and easy once established, it roots readily from single-node cuttings.
sources: Costa Farms Plant Finder — Baltic Blue Pothos
Royal Horticultural Society — Epipremnum pinnatum 'Baltic Blue'

planting.note: Needs years of uninterrupted climbing growth on a moss pole or trellis in warm, bright indirect light before it produces its namesake perforated adult leaves; keep temperatures above 65°F for steady progression.

directions: 'Skeleton Key' is grown for its architectural mature-form leaves, which emerge narrow and lance-shaped and progressively develop paired, symmetrical, keyhole-shaped perforations flanking the midrib as the plant ages on a climbing support — a distinctly different fenestration pattern from the ragged lobing of the plain species or the early edge-splitting of 'Baltic Blue.' Young plants often show light cream or pale-yellow marbling along the leaf margins, but this variegation is unstable and commonly fades to solid green as the leaves mature and the plant's energy goes into producing its elaborate perforated form. Reaching full 'skeleton key' leaf character indoors typically takes several years of vigorous, well-supported climbing growth rather than trailing culture. Propagate from stem cuttings taken below a node.
sources: Plant Addicts — Skeleton Key Pothos care guide
